extracted.intended_audience: scholars, students, and critics studying ethnic humor, sociology of humor, and cultural analysts
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Davies's framework to identify whether an instance of ethnic humor fits the 'stupid' or 'canny' pattern (or neither), determine the social relation between joke-teller and target, and interpret the joke's social function in terms of anxieties about material interest and modernity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stupid pattern (characteristics of 'stupid' jokes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes about 'stupid' minorities: the target is typically rural, peripheral, or lower-status; geographically adjacent but seen as lagging. The same target is told to fail at simple tasks, not understand modern technology, or interpret things literally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Polish jokes (US), Belgian jokes (France), Irish jokes (England), East Frisian jokes (Germany), Newfie jokes (Canada). Look for narratives of failing at simple tasks, misunderstanding modern life, or literal-mindedness. This pattern vastly outnumbers other types in Davies's catalogue; use presence of these narrative features as markers. Anti-pattern: treating any insult as 'stupid pattern' without checking the target's peripheral/social status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canny pattern (characteristics of 'canny' jokes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes about 'canny' or stingy minorities: the target is typically a traditionally commercial, mercantile, or financial-specialized group, often diasporic; the jokes feature miserliness and cleverness in money matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Jewish jokes (Europe/US), Scottish jokes (England), Genoese jokes (Italy), Aberdeen jokes within Scotland. Look for plot elements prioritizing material gain, bargaining, or extreme thrift. Distinguish from neutral praise for shrewdness by the moral framing: canny is cast as a moral failing (materialism overriding other values).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern classification: stupid, canny, or neither
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether an ethnic joke follows the stupid pattern, the canny pattern, or neither.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use narrative content (failure-of-material-interest vs excess-of-material-interest), the social position of the target, and typical motifs to classify. Davies recommends starting analysis by identifying which pattern, if any, the joke exemplifies. If it lacks both failure and excess themes or targets different dynamics, classify it as 'neither' and consider other explanatory frameworks (e.g., genuine hostility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify social position of the target relative to the joke-teller
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify whether the named target is peripheral/rural/lower-status (stupid pattern) or diasporic/mercantile (canny pattern), and more generally the target's social relation to the joke-teller.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess geography (adjacent/peripheral), economic role (commercial vs noncommercial), social status, and whether the group is diasporic. This relational position is crucial: the pattern presupposes a joke-teller positioned between peripheral and diasporic groups. If the target is a dominant majority, Davies's pattern likely does not apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive frame: jokes as expressions of the joke-teller's anxieties
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret whether the joke is structurally about the joke-teller's anxieties balancing material gain and other values, rather than straightforward condemnation of the target's traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for evidence that the joke projects concerns about modern industrial life and material interest onto targets: the 'stupid' fails to look after material interest; the 'canny' sacrifices other values for material interest. Corroborating signs include the same tellers telling both kinds of jokes and jokes' popularity among people with positive relations to the target. Treat this interpretation as Davies's 'deflationary insight' and consider it when attributing motive or hostility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish ethnic stupid/canny jokes from genuine hate-driven humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether a joke represents the stupid/canny structural pattern (focused on material-interest anxieties) or whether it is genuine hostile/hate humor that functions differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genuine hate humor will often lack the stupid/canny mirror-image structure, may target majority/dominant groups differently, and may be motivated by overt hostility rather than the joke-teller's ambivalence. Use markers: absence of mirroring (both stupid and canny), lack of cross-target switching by same tellers, and explicit dehumanizing or exclusionary content as signals of genuine hostility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for the cross-cultural script invariance
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether the same joke script (structure) is told about different named targets in different cultures — i.e., structure constant, named target varies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Davies notes light-bulb jokes and other scripts migrate across cultures with only the target label changing. Evidence of script invariance supports reading the joke as performing a relational function (positioning the joke-teller) rather than expressing a fixed attribute of that particular target. Use cross-cultural comparison and historical shifts in targets as supporting data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify the social conditions required for the stupid/canny pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirm whether the societal conditions Davies identifies are present: (1) a modernizing/industrializing society with a capitalist economy, (2) an identifiable peripheral group seen as falling behind modernity, (3) an identifiable diasporic group exemplifying market values, and (4) joke-tellers positioned between these extremes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If these conditions do not obtain in the society under study, Davies predicts the stupid/canny pattern will not form. Treat these as necessary contextual preconditions rather than optional background. Use historical and socioeconomic data to assess presence of these conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess motif-specific features (failure vs excess of material interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the joke expresses a failure to look after one's material interest (stupid motif) or an excessive preoccupation with material interest (canny motif).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look at punchline logic: does humor derive from incompetence/naiveté about material welfare, or from obsessive thrift/cheatiness? This functional distinction is central to Davies's taxonomy and should guide classification and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider teller-target relations and shifting targets
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the same individuals tell jokes about both stupid and canny groups, and whether targets shift across generations — evidence that jokes reflect teller anxieties rather than fixed antipathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of both patterns in a teller's repertoire and historical target shifts support Davies's claim that the humor is a reflexive social mechanism. Absence of such evidence weakens the deflationary interpretation and suggests alternative explanations (e.g., entrenched prejudice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope limitation: the pattern excludes majority-dominant targets and obvious hate humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that Davies's stupid/canny pattern presupposes targeting peripheral or diasporic minorities; it does not apply to jokes about majority/dominant groups or to explicit hate humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before applying Davies's framework, rule out whether the target is a majority or whether the joke is explicitly hostile/dehumanizing. If so, apply other analytical frameworks. This is both a diagnostic exclusion and a boundary condition for the framework's validity.
